My first PR to Mathlib: #45116. The rank of a matrix over a field is at least k iff it has a nonzero k × k minor, allowing infinitely many rows.

Extracted from my CCDN formalisation project https://github.com/jasondavies/ccdn-dimension-growth, labelled LLM-generated, and would welcome a review. Thanks!
Auto-closed by a bot for use of AI :( Can anyone explain why?
My guess is that something in my comment triggered the AI flag -- possibly the copy/paste of Unicode maths characters?

Basically, the issue is that it isn't a good use of reviewer time to review new-contributor PRs where the code and subsequent revisions are AI-generated.

Reviewer bandwidth is extremely limited (currently over 600 PRs on queue). For most new-contributor PRs, it would be faster for the reviewer to do the work themselves to the desired standard than to go through several review cycles of reading through the PR and suggesting improvements. But we review new-contributor PRs anyway because it's one of the best ways to help people get better at Lean and learn how to write for mathlib (indeed, we were all there once!). But if code and revisions are being written by AI, then that negates most of this benefit.

So if you'd like to learn the language yourself, then we'd be more than happy to help review your PRs! (even if they're initially far below what AI can write nowdays)
Perhaps to get started you could share what you're passionate about, and we could suggest small projects in those areas?

Right now most of my projects are in the area of elementary and algorithmic number theory (GCD and related algorithms). So potentially more appropriate for CSLib?

All of my formalisation projects so far have been auto-generated, but they've all been related to GCD algorithms, or are intended to support formalisations of said algorithms. The CCDN project came about because of this (relating to unpublished work). When refactoring, I generated a ForMathlib/ directory and that's where the rank via nonzero minors came from.

For a small beginner project that I could do entirely by hand, how about something like Lamé's theorem or binary GCD? There's a Lamé's theorem PR but work has stalled: #37584

I guess my secondary interest is linear algebra. One idea is something to do with determinants of a circulant matrix. Also I don't know if you'd consider another attempt at rank via nonzero minors if I write it by hand from scratch, perhaps with a smaller scope?

IMO Lamé's theorem and other algorithmic stuff are indeed more fit for CSLib, although opinions vary.
(there are still CS results in Mathlib, and e.g. we have primality checking algorithms)

If you're interested I think there's lots of algebra we're missing to support algebraic algorithms, such as stuff about resultants or Hensel lifting or Gröbner bases (some of these have open PRs w/ partial progress).

As for linear algebra I'd love to have that rank result (btw also Sylvester's criterion), but I would encourage you to first think about the correct generality, and if and how we could get each proof to be roughly one line. I think there's a learning curve to understanding Mathlib's philosophy, and getting PR reviews and processing them yourself is a good way to learn.

I'd suggest considering some goal (e.g. the rank result) and trying to work towards it manually. Along the way you'll notice that some things are annoying to do, and if only you had some small unrelated lemma the next step in the proof would've been much neater. Then you also get better at using Loogle (or #Is there code for X?) to find small lemmas, and you'll probably find tons of such small missing stuff, and then you could start contributing and get feedback, and at a certain point you could PR the big result.
Other good ways to onboard are to read existing code, review PRs by others on stuff in areas you feel comfortable with, and also going through undergrad books to find results we're missing (of which there are surprisingly many).

Specifically about the rank thing: are you sure that CommRing + IsDomain is the best possible? There are lots of other typeclasses: maybe HasRankNullity or other ring properties are the correct assumptions?
Also about the proofs themselves, IMO we shouldn't go through the fraction field when possible (and I'm pretty sure a direct proof is possible here) unless the alternative looks worse.

Gustas Mickus said:

What would be the best way to proceed here? Should I put the draft aside and try rewriting the proofs completely by hand from scratch (perhaps starting with a smaller scope), or would you recommend starting with an even simpler, unrelated project first?

See what I said above about doing lots of small stuff to gain experience.
About the specific result, it might be the case that there's no way to get good looking proofs of truncating things, though I'm not sure. E.g. #44214 which truncates Taylor series looks rather long, but bounds for π and e look pretty nice.
So regardless I'd recommend going with something nicer first. How long is your draft, and how long is each theorem? You could similarly post in #new members about your interests and ask for suggestions.
(we're in a thread about a specific PR, which is unrelated)
I see you've suggested a new definition before, but probably starting with theorems is much easier.

If that wasn't clear enough from the above comments, we don't like LLM-generated code from new contributors very much, but we absolutely hate new contributors feeding our reviews into an LLM to further modify their PR

I would therefore suggest you prioritise learning from the feedback we provide and make an effort to implement it by hand, even if the code is originally AI-generated. Of course, writing the original code by hand makes it easier for you to modify it further following reviews, but you should decide yourself whether this matters
